Vellum Milestone 1 delivery report
Implementation for Vellum’s first grant milestone is complete and ready for community review.
M1 established the foundation for portable reputation on did:ckb: the Claim Cell contracts are deployed on CKB Testnet, @usevellum/sdk is published with Claim Cell read and write APIs, all four planned account-verification flows can issue claims through Vellum’s Testnet issuer, the schema registry is published, and the dashboard computes a transparent score from the resulting on-chain evidence.
Repository: GitHub - truthixify/vellum: Portable identity and verifiable reputation for builders on Nervos CKB. · GitHub
Live website: https://usevellum.xyz
Live dashboard: https://dashboard.usevellum.xyz
Approved proposal and report thread: [DIS] Vellum: Reputation Extension on did:ckb
Public roadmap: Vellum Reputation Extension · GitHub
M1 issue and pull request record: GitHub · Where software is built
Delivery against the proposal
Approved M1 deliverable
Result
Claim Cell Type Script deployed on CKB Testnet at a published address
Complete. Claim Type and the separate reusable DID Lock are live as independent Type ID code cells.
readClaims and writeClaim SDK additions
Complete and published in the Vellum-owned @usevellum/sdk package. The ownership change from the original upstream-package plan is explained below.
Verified-social claim issuance for GitHub, Discord, Telegram, and Bluesky
Complete. Each flow verifies account control, binds issuance to a wallet-proven subject DID, and submits Claim Cells through the configured Vellum issuer.
Schema specifications documented and published
Complete. Seven immutable v1 schema manifests, hashes, parsers, examples, and specifications are published.
The GitHub milestone now has no open implementation items. It records 16 completed issues and 16 merged milestone pull requests covering the protocol, contracts, deployment, SDK, verification service, scoring policy, schemas, and dashboard. Final npm publication followed through pull requests #50 and #51.
What shipped
Claim Cell protocol and Testnet contracts
Vellum now has a small on-chain assertion format built around two CKB scripts:
Claim Type validates canonical Claim data, fresh authorization from the current controller of the issuer’s did:ckb, timestamps, unique claim IDs, schema binding, and the subject lock.
DID Lock lets a Claim Cell remain attached to a stable did:ckb identity while following controller rotation. Claim Type can also accept another complete CKB lock when an integration chooses that subject model.
The final protocol does not use a detached issuer signature. The issuer’s current controller lock authorizes the complete CKB transaction, and the subject controls the output Cell. A holder can consume a claim they no longer want to retain and recover its capacity.
Both contracts are deployed in one CKB Testnet transaction while retaining independent Type ID identities and upgrade paths:
Deployment transaction: https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0xaf693346282063a5d51f79d180fc807cdba1b8ac9d7af30085ff0aa190e2686c
Claim Type: output 0x0, code hash 0xfb2757e524b3f83161d8b85b8b3e00186e2019ff04f5dfe833c5a72731e13157
DID Lock: output 0x1, code hash 0xe1562cc57b4bd91619ada2f7e74d63805ea7038a7b6de0b18a529d51aa883d2d
Machine-readable deployment record: vellum/deployments/testnet.json at main · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
Protocol specification: vellum/docs/claim-cell.md at main · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
Fresh release builds are compared byte for byte with the live Testnet code cells. The current Claim Type binary is 47,752 bytes and the DID Lock is 30,336 bytes. Measured Claim Type paths range from 14,964 cycles for destruction to 146,842 cycles for creation with issuer replacement.
Claim SDK
The Vellum SDK now provides typed Claim Cell codecs and the two main integration paths:
readClaims scans every indexer page for an exact subject lock, supports issuer and schema filters, decodes Molecule and canonical DAG-CBOR, evaluates expiry at an explicit application checkpoint, and reports malformed or unverifiable evidence without silently accepting it.
writeClaim and writeClaims build prepared, balanced, unsigned transactions with dynamic capacity calculation, fresh issuer-controller authorization, explicit payer behavior, and stable output metadata. Signing and broadcasting remain explicit caller actions.
The live Testnet suite covers same-issuer and cross-issuer reads, single and atomic batch construction, and holder-controlled claim destruction with capacity recovery. Public fixtures include:
Known live claim: https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0x9e32511bcaa49d89421d070d28eded7168fa9010a007659151e7f8928caff91c
Cross-issuer claim: https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0xdd3ba6f4574568df0f82a1a9201598da697ff4ce28b3b1cc7a28289ef2319cb3
Claim creation and later capacity recovery: https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0x6003e4e13d757a02003cc23d156f100ff351ca28f0d67df7f04bf71d18255640 and https://testnet.explorer.nervos.org/transaction/0x647a5253321acb45e8aa07195f0414678831f955610bdfcce59efa1107638816
SDK guide: vellum/docs/claim-sdk.md at main · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
Package guide: vellum/packages/sdk/README.md at main · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
npm package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@usevellum/sdk
GitHub release: Release @usevellum/sdk@0.1.0 · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
Version 0.1.0 is available from npm. A Changesets-based GitHub workflow validates and packs release candidates, publishes approved releases, and creates the matching Git tag and GitHub release.
Verification, issuance, and reputation
The dashboard runs a server-side verification and issuance service on Vercel. The connected wallet proves control of the selected subject DID; Vellum’s published Testnet issuer authorizes, funds, and submits the Claim Cell transaction. OAuth credentials, OIDC tokens, and app passwords are transient and are not stored as reputation data.
The four planned account sources are live:
GitHub: verifies the stable account and can issue separate evidence for qualifying public work in reviewed CKB ecosystem repositories.
Discord: verifies the stable account and can issue separate membership evidence for configured CKB communities and roles.
Telegram: verifies the stable account through Telegram OIDC and can issue current membership evidence for configured Nervos groups where the Vellum bot is an administrator.
Bluesky: authenticates with a scoped app password, resolves the stable AT Protocol DID, closes the temporary session, and issues the identity claim.
The issuer identity and transaction policy are public at https://dashboard.usevellum.xyz/api/issuer. The current issuer is did:ckb:hlvxrdt3e7iwvuxdmbvejp6hc4yoo3no on CKB Testnet.
The read-only scoring service applies the frozen vellum.reputation.v5 policy on demand. It returns an integer score out of 1,000 across Technical, Contribution, Community, Tenure, and Recency, together with the exact Claim Cells and policy rules behind every point. Duplicate, superseded, expired, untrusted, or malformed evidence cannot contribute silently, and incomplete chain state returns unavailable rather than a partial score. There is no private reputation database and no opaque score claim.
Verification service documentation: vellum/docs/verification-service.md at main · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
Scoring policy and API: vellum/docs/reputation-scoring.md at main · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
Live verification UI: Vellum Dashboard - Identity and reputation on CKB
Live reputation UI: Vellum Dashboard - Identity and reputation on CKB
Published schemas and dashboard
Seven current verifier outputs have immutable v1 specifications, canonical JSON manifests, pinned CKB hashes, typed parsers, and validated examples:
vellum.social.github.v1
vellum.contribution.github.v1
vellum.social.discord.v1
vellum.community.discord.v1
vellum.social.telegram.v1
vellum.community.telegram.v1
vellum.social.bluesky.v1
Registry: vellum/docs/schemas at main · truthixify/vellum · GitHub
The dashboard now exposes the selected identity’s aggregate score throughout the live experience, provides a public evidence breakdown and share card, shows every Claim Cell returned by verification, and keeps later issuance and governance work out of the live M1 navigation. The public site and dashboard also share one app identity and follow the system theme until the user chooses an explicit override.
Implementation evidence
Workstream
Merged pull requests
Protocol, contracts, and deployment
#31 protocol, #32 contracts, #33 Testnet deployment
SDK
#34 API design, #35 reader, #36 writer, #37 package preparation, #50 release automation, #51 v0.1.0 release
Verification and scoring
#38 service, #40 GitHub identity, #41 scoring, #43 Discord, #44 GitHub contributions, #45 Telegram, #46 Bluesky
Schemas and product review
#47 schema registry, #49 dashboard consistency
The Claim Cell protocol and SDK boundary both received independent public review before M1 delivery was finalized. Review findings changed the design materially, including separating Claim Type from DID Lock, accepting arbitrary CKB subject locks, removing reusable detached claim signatures, tightening issuer-history handling, and clarifying package ownership. The protocol review is recorded in Vellum PR #31, and the package-boundary review is recorded in CCC PR #562.
Verification results
The final M1 pull request CI run is public at Release @usevellum/sdk · truthixify/vellum@451a36a · GitHub and passed both jobs.
326 Bun/TypeScript tests passed across 53 files with 0 failures and 1,105 assertions.
Formatting, ESLint, strict TypeScript checks, both Vite production builds, executable SDK examples, and package inspection passed.
21 Rust parser and CKB-VM integration tests passed for Claim Type and DID Lock.
Six public CKB Testnet SDK checks passed against committed on-chain fixtures.
The deployment verifier rebuilt both contracts and matched every byte, hash, capacity, Type ID, and locator against the live code cells.
The final dashboard audit passed 138 responsive route checks across 390 px, 768 px, and 1440 px in both themes. A separate 10-case browser pass verified system-theme changes and manual overrides in both applications.
The release workflow at Merge pull request #51 from truthixify/changeset-release/main · truthixify/vellum@e60bee3 · GitHub validated, packed, and published @usevellum/sdk@0.1.0, then created the matching GitHub release.
Changes from the original implementation plan
One ownership boundary changed after review. The proposal placed readClaims and writeClaim in @ckb-ccc/did-ckb. CCC PR #562 presented that implementation for upstream review, and the maintainer recommended a standalone Vellum SDK because the Claim protocol is application-specific and not used elsewhere in CCC. The PR was closed after that recommendation was accepted. The final design keeps DID identifier and identity primitives in @ckb-ccc/did-ckb, while Claim Cell codecs, readers, transaction builders, release ownership, and Vellum policy live in the Vellum-owned @usevellum/sdk package. This preserves the small integration surface promised in the proposal without coupling the general DID package to Vellum’s protocol. @usevellum/sdk@0.1.0 is now published on npm; generic CCC utilities can still be contributed upstream separately when a concrete reusable need is identified.
The proposal also used “OAuth” as shorthand for every social connection. The implementation uses the appropriate provider mechanism instead: OAuth for GitHub and Discord, OIDC for Telegram, and a scoped app password plus stable-DID resolution for Bluesky.
Finally, issuance and scoring are deliberately separate. The verification service issues factual Claim Cells; the scoring service reads those Cells and applies a versioned policy on demand. This keeps the evidence portable and lets another application apply a different policy without depending on a Vellum-owned score record.
Testing, feedback, and review
M1 is live on CKB Testnet, and community testing would be useful before the milestone is confirmed:
Inspect the public score and evidence for did:ckb:4kiidiczwthgxj7dltzkzopgbwu3v6jc at Vellum Dashboard - Identity and reputation on CKB.
Connect a CKB Testnet wallet at Vellum Dashboard - Identity and reputation on CKB and test one of the GitHub, Discord, Telegram, or Bluesky verification flows against a DID the wallet controls.
Install @usevellum/sdk and try the documented Claim Cell read or transaction-building APIs.
Please share test results, unexpected behavior, integration questions, or other feedback in this thread or through Issues · truthixify/vellum · GitHub. I am also requesting review of the delivery evidence above and the designated reviewer sign-off required to confirm M1.
Next milestone
M2 moves from the foundation to the public builder record: richer public profile pages, reusable schema renderers, the CKBoost integration and claim format, and continued website and documentation work. The Claim Cell, SDK, verification, and scoring foundation delivered here is what those surfaces will read and extend.
Thank you to everyone who reviewed the protocol and SDK, tested the verification flows, and raised issues during implementation. Questions and independent checks of the linked evidence are welcome.

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text: My two cents, one service that needs the node itself is serving light clients. It runs over the node’s own p2p protocol, so it cannot be served from someone else’s RPC, and CKB nodes already do it for free, since light client support is on by default. Wallets that embed a light client depend on it. A fee there would go to the node itself, not to a server next to it, and it looks like a natural fit for Jan’s idea in the related thread of paying per data served over Fiber.

recent_posts.topic_title: A Revenue Layer for CKB Nodes
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks, a good example of a service that only a real, synced full node can provide, and every node already runs it. But I’d be careful: light clients depend on it, so the basic service should stay free, or wallets break. A fee could only work as an optional extra on top, e.g. priority or higher limits for wallet providers, maybe paid per data via Fiber as @janx suggested.
It brings me back to the core idea: full nodes offering side services for a fee, paid in CKB or via Fiber. Applications and their users pay for a service they need, and nodes earn by doing the work. A win-win.
Some services depend on a full node by nature (light clients, attestations about chain state). Others, like storage or event watching, could technically run on any server. My proposal is to make a full node a requirement for every service anyway. An app would then know its service runs on a synced node that verifies the chain itself, not on a script reading someone else’s RPC. That raises trust for all services, and it gives people a reason to run more full nodes.
The hard part is proving it: how does an app know the service really runs on a full node? Ideas welcome.
